exercise.title: Why is an instantaneous rate a limit rather than a ratio?

statement.p: The difference quotient \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is an average rate. In your own words, why must h approach 0 rather than be set equal to 0, and what idea does the resulting limit name?

hint.p: Setting h=0 divides by zero. The instantaneous rate is the value the averages settle toward, not a value obtained by plugging in.

paragraphs.title: A tangent line can cross the curve
paragraphs.p: It is tempting to say that a tangent line is a line that touches the graph at one point and does not cross it. That picture works for some curves, but it is not a definition.

But the graph of y=x^3 crosses this line at the origin. The tangent line is still correct because its slope is the limiting secant slope.

exercise.title: Why is a tangent a limiting secant rather than a line that merely touches?

statement.p: As h\to 0, secant slopes may approach a single number, which we call the tangent slope. In your own words, why is touches at one point and does not cross an unreliable definition, and what example in this section shows the trouble?

hint.p: Look at y=x^3 at the origin. The tangent line is still the limiting position of secants even if the curve crosses it.

subsection.title: The derivative as a limit
subsection.p: The derivative is a limit of slopes:
This formula has three layers.
First, the quotient
is an average rate of change over an interval.
Second, the limit
shrinks the interval toward a single input.
Third, the result f'(a), if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change at a.
The limit must exist as one finite number. If the slopes approach different values from different sides, there is no derivative.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: the corner in |x|
paragraphs.p: The right-side slopes approach 1. The left-side slopes approach -1. There is no single limiting slope.

figure.caption: At a corner, the left and right limiting slopes can disagree. Then the derivative does not exist.

paragraphs.p: The graph has a sharp corner at the origin. The corner is not the real reason the derivative fails; it is the picture of the reason. The reason is that the limiting slopes do not approach one common value.

note.title: What can go wrong?
note.p: The derivative at a exists only when
If the left and right slopes disagree, or if the slopes grow without bound, then f'(a) does not exist.

paragraphs.p: One derivative gives one slope at one point. But a curve has many points. If we let the point a move, the derivative itself becomes a new function. That new function will tell us how the whole graph is changing.

exercise.title: Why does a corner prevent a derivative?

statement.p: For f(x)=|x|, the right-hand slopes near 0 approach 1 and the left-hand slopes approach -1. In your own words, why does that disagreement mean f'(0) does not exist, and why is the corner a picture of that reason rather than a separate reason?

hint.p: A derivative at a point must be one finite limiting slope. If the two sides settle toward different numbers, there is no such number.
